title: Home Medication Reconciliation: Find the Duplicate, Omission, and Unsafe Combination
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Home medication reconciliation compares what the patient actually takes with the current prescribed list, including OTC drugs, supplements, duplicate bottles, stopped medications, and recent discharge changes.
recognize: Multiple bottles of the same drug, old prescriptions, different strengths, and patient-created schedules are common hazards.
Transitions of care are high-risk periods for omissions and duplication.
priorities: Build one accurate list and clarify discrepancies through the appropriate prescriber/pharmacist/RN channel.
Escalate high-risk discrepancies involving anticoagulants, insulin, opioids, seizure medications, or cardiovascular drugs.
assessMonitor: Actual bottles, dose, frequency, indication, adherence, adverse effects, cognition, vision, dexterity, and pharmacy use.
interventions: Use teach-back and a simplified current list; remove discontinued drugs from active use when directed.
medicationSafety: Never assume the electronic list matches what is in the home.
teaching: Keep one current medication list and bring it to every appointment.
delegationScope: Medication reconciliation requires licensed review and escalation; nonlicensed staff may collect bottle information but should not resolve discrepancies independently.
examTrap: Copying the discharge medication list without comparing it with what the patient is actually taking.
oneLinePearl: Reconcile the bottles, not just the chart.

title: Home Oxygen Safety: Oxygen Feeds Fire
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Home oxygen increases fire intensity. Smoking, open flame, petroleum-based products near oxygen equipment, and unsafe storage are preventable hazards.
recognize: Burn marks, active smoking, candles, gas stoves used unsafely, extension-cord overload, or unsecured cylinders increase risk.
Tubing creates trip hazards and may kink or disconnect.
priorities: Remove ignition hazards and reinforce no-smoking/no-open-flame rules.
Escalate unsafe conditions that cannot be corrected, especially when vulnerable household members are at risk.
assessMonitor: Equipment function, prescribed flow, tubing, skin pressure points, fire risks, electrical safety, and patient understanding.
interventions: Secure cylinders, maintain clear pathways, and use only prescribed flow/settings.
medicationSafety: Oxygen is a prescribed therapy; patients should not alter flow based solely on symptoms without a plan.
redFlags: Smoking while oxygen is in use
teaching: Keep oxygen away from flames and heat sources and post no-smoking signs when appropriate.
delegationScope: Routine equipment observations may be delegated; clinical deterioration and unsafe therapy settings require licensed escalation.
examTrap: Focusing only on SpO2 while ignoring a lit cigarette beside the oxygen concentrator.
oneLinePearl: Home oxygen is a treatment—and a fire hazard if handled poorly.
sourceBasis: American Lung Association home oxygen safety principles

title: Home Wound Surveillance: Know When Routine Drainage Becomes Infection
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Home wound care depends on trend recognition: increasing pain, erythema, warmth, swelling, purulent drainage, odor, fever, or wound separation requires escalation rather than simply changing the dressing again.
recognize: Some drainage may be expected depending on wound type and stage, but worsening local/systemic signs are concerning.
Older or immunocompromised adults may have subtle systemic symptoms.
priorities: Assess the wound and patient together, not the dressing alone.
Escalate systemic illness, rapidly spreading erythema, necrosis, or dehiscence.
assessMonitor: Size/depth if ordered, tissue appearance, drainage amount/color/odor, surrounding skin, pain, temperature, glucose control, nutrition.
interventions: Perform ordered wound care using clean/sterile technique as indicated and protect periwound skin.
medicationSafety: Antibiotics should be taken exactly as prescribed; topical agents should not be added without direction.
teaching: Report worsening pain, drainage, odor, redness, fever, or opening of the wound.
delegationScope: Wound-care scope varies by state/facility; abnormal wound assessment and escalation require licensed judgment.
examTrap: Continuing routine dressing changes despite progressive redness, pain, and fever.
oneLinePearl: A wound trend can deteriorate before a single dramatic sign appears.

title: Diabetes Sick-Day Safety at Home: Prevent DKA, HHS, and Hypoglycemia
bottomLine: Illness can raise glucose even when intake falls. Sick-day plans should specify glucose/ketone monitoring, hydration, medication rules, and thresholds for urgent help rather than telling patients to stop all diabetes medication automatically.
recognize: Persistent hyperglycemia, vomiting, dehydration, ketones, altered mentation, or inability to keep fluids down are danger signs.
Reduced intake can also cause hypoglycemia depending on medications.
priorities: Follow the individualized sick-day plan and maintain hydration when safe.
Escalate vomiting, ketones with illness, severe hyperglycemia, recurrent hypoglycemia, or altered mental status.
assessMonitor: Glucose trend, ketones when directed, hydration, intake, urine output, medication use, symptoms.
interventions: Reinforce prescribed monitoring frequency and carbohydrate/fluid strategies.
medicationSafety: Insulin should not be reflexively stopped; SGLT2 inhibitors and some other agents have illness-specific hold considerations per prescriber plan.
teaching: Keep written sick-day instructions and emergency contact thresholds available.
delegationScope: Teaching reinforcement is within PN scope when based on an established plan; medication-plan changes require authorized clinician input.
examTrap: Telling every ill patient with diabetes to stop insulin because they are not eating normally.
oneLinePearl: Sick days require more monitoring, not less.
sourceBasis: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026

title: Heart Failure at Home: Act on Weight and Breathing Trends Early
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Home heart-failure care relies on daily trends in weight, dyspnea, orthopnea, edema, fatigue, BP, and medication adherence. The action plan—not a memorized universal weight number—should define when to call.
recognize: New orthopnea, reduced activity tolerance, rapid weight gain, edema, or increasing diuretic need can indicate worsening congestion.
Dizziness, confusion, oliguria, or hypotension can indicate poor perfusion or overdiuresis.
priorities: Compare symptoms with the patient's baseline and individualized action plan.
Escalate rest dyspnea, chest pain, syncope, or rapid deterioration.
assessMonitor: Daily weight, edema, breathing, BP/HR, urine output, adherence, diet/fluid plan.
interventions: Reinforce prescribed sodium/fluid and medication plan and early contact thresholds.
medicationSafety: Do not independently double diuretics unless the written plan specifically authorizes it.
teaching: Weigh under consistent conditions and follow individualized call thresholds.
delegationScope: Weight collection may be delegated; interpretation and escalation remain licensed responsibilities.
examTrap: Waiting for severe edema before reporting progressive orthopnea and weight gain.
oneLinePearl: Home heart failure is managed by trends plus an action plan.
sourceBasis: American Heart Association heart failure self-monitoring resources

title: Home Fall-Risk Assessment: Fix the Environment and the Physiology
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Home fall prevention requires both environmental correction and clinical review of balance, orthostasis, vision, footwear, cognition, medications, and assistive-device use.
recognize: Loose rugs, clutter, poor lighting, stairs without rails, bathroom hazards, pets, and oxygen tubing can combine with physiologic risk.
Sedatives, hypotension, neuropathy, and urgency/nocturia increase risk.
priorities: Address modifiable hazards and communicate new clinical fall risks.
Escalate recurrent unexplained falls, syncope, or new neurologic findings.
assessMonitor: Fall history, gait, orthostasis, vision, footwear, cognition, medications, bathroom/stair safety.
interventions: Recommend appropriate lighting, grab bars/rails, clear pathways, correct assistive devices, and supervision as needed.
medicationSafety: Medication review is essential; do not independently discontinue drugs.
teaching: Use prescribed mobility aids every time, not only when feeling weak.
delegationScope: Environmental observations may be delegated; clinical fall-risk interpretation requires licensed review.
examTrap: Removing one rug and declaring the fall risk solved while ignoring orthostatic hypotension and sedatives.
oneLinePearl: Falls come from the person plus the environment.

title: Caregiver Strain: A Safety Issue, Not Just Stress
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Caregiver exhaustion can affect medication accuracy, nutrition, hygiene, supervision, and abuse/neglect risk. Assess the caregiver's capacity as part of patient safety.
recognize: Sleep deprivation, resentment, missed medications, unsafe lifting, inability to leave the patient alone, financial strain, or statements of hopelessness signal burden.
Caregiver distress does not automatically equal abuse, but it can increase risk.
priorities: Identify immediate safety concerns and available support/respite resources.
Escalate suspected abuse/neglect according to law and policy.
assessMonitor: Caregiver capacity, sleep, mood, physical health, support network, patient dependency, medication/care errors.
interventions: Connect with social work/case management, respite, community resources, and realistic care plans.
medicationSafety: Complex medication regimens may need simplification or pharmacy supports through the care team.
teaching: Seeking respite is a safety strategy, not a failure.
delegationScope: Social/resource referrals vary by role; mandatory reporting duties vary by state and population and must follow law/policy.
examTrap: Focusing only on the patient's needs while ignoring an exhausted caregiver who cannot safely provide care.
oneLinePearl: A collapsing caregiver can become a patient-safety emergency.
sourceBasis: Administration for Community Living caregiver-support principles

title: Home Infection Prevention: Clean Technique Still Requires Discipline
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Home care often uses clean rather than hospital-sterile technique for selected tasks, but hand hygiene, equipment cleaning, safe sharps disposal, catheter/line precautions, and contamination prevention remain essential.
recognize: Shared supplies, pets, cluttered surfaces, reused single-use items, poor hand hygiene, and unsafe sharps containers create avoidable risk.
Patients with central lines, urinary catheters, wounds, or immunosuppression need stricter adherence to prescribed technique.
priorities: Perform hand hygiene and prepare a clean work area before care.
Escalate signs of device- or wound-associated infection promptly.
assessMonitor: Care environment, hand hygiene, supply storage, line/catheter/wound sites, sharps disposal.
interventions: Use prescribed technique and single-use supplies correctly; clean reusable equipment per instructions.
medicationSafety: Injection supplies and multidose products must be handled according to labeling and infection-control standards.
teaching: Do not reuse needles/syringes and keep supplies clean, dry, and separated from contaminants.
delegationScope: Technique requirements depend on task and policy; invasive device care may require specific licensure/competency.
examTrap: Assuming infection prevention is less important because the setting is a private home.
oneLinePearl: Home is not sterile, but technique still matters.

title: Home Emergency Planning: Know Who to Call Before the Crisis
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: High-risk home-care patients need a written emergency plan covering symptoms that require 911, clinician call thresholds, medication/equipment needs, power outages, evacuation, and caregiver backup.
recognize: Oxygen concentrators, ventilatory support, refrigerated medications, mobility dependence, or cognitive impairment increase disaster vulnerability.
Families may know routine care but not when a change exceeds home management.
priorities: Clarify emergency symptoms and backup plans before discharge/home admission.
Ensure emergency contacts and essential information are accessible.
assessMonitor: Equipment dependence, power backup, transportation, mobility, communication ability, medication supply, caregiver availability.
interventions: Use written plans and teach-back; coordinate community emergency resources as appropriate.
medicationSafety: Plan safe storage and backup for time-sensitive/refrigerated/high-alert medications.
teaching: Know which symptoms mean call 911 versus call the clinic.
delegationScope: Emergency-planning coordination may involve the interdisciplinary team; PN reinforces the established plan and reports gaps.
examTrap: Assuming the family will improvise safely during a power outage or acute deterioration.
oneLinePearl: A home emergency plan is part of the treatment plan.

title: Change in Condition at Home: Do Not Normalize Deterioration
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: In home and long-term care, subtle changes—new confusion, reduced intake, weakness, falls, dyspnea, oliguria, or functional decline—may be the earliest sign of acute illness. Compare with baseline and escalate rather than attributing everything to age or chronic disease.
recognize: Older adults may show delirium, falls, anorexia, or decline before classic fever or focal symptoms.
Caregiver concern that 'something is different' is meaningful clinical data.
priorities: Assess ABCs, vital signs, mental/functional change, hydration, pain, medications, and likely triggers.
Activate EMS for severe instability; otherwise notify the appropriate RN/provider promptly.
assessMonitor: Baseline versus current cognition, function, vitals, intake/output, respiratory status, pain, medication changes.
interventions: Provide immediate safety/support within orders and document the change and escalation response.
medicationSafety: Review recent medication additions/dose changes as potential contributors without assuming they are the only cause.
teaching: Families should report sudden changes in thinking, breathing, intake, mobility, or urine output.
delegationScope: Observation can be shared, but interpretation and escalation of a change in condition are licensed responsibilities.
examTrap: Calling a new acute decline 'normal aging.'
oneLinePearl: Baseline change is a vital sign in home care.
sourceBasis: CMS change-in-condition and long-term-care safety principles
